name: Invoice Capture and Coding
title: Invoice Capture and Coding
answer: Invoice capture and coding covers the intake of supplier invoices from any channel, including paper, PDF, email, and electronic data interchange, and the extraction of header and line-level data such as vendor, date, amount, tax, and purchase order references. It also covers the assignment of accounting codes, including general ledger accounts, cost centers, projects, and tax codes, so that the invoice can be posted and paid. The scope includes validation against purchase orders and vendor master records, exception handling for missing or mismatched data, and the audit trail that links each coded invoice back to its source document. In practice, this work sits inside accounts payable and feeds directly into the general ledger and payment run.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Invoice capture and coding covers the intake of supplier invoices from any channel, including paper, PDF, email, and electronic data interchange, and the extraction of header and line-level data such as vendor, date, amount, tax, and purchase order references. It also covers the assignment of accounting codes, including general ledger accounts, cost centers, projects, and tax codes, so that the invoice can be posted and paid. The scope includes validation against purchase orders and vendor master records, exception handling for missing or mismatched data, and the audit trail that links each coded invoice back to its source document. In practice, this work sits inside accounts payable and feeds directly into the general ledger and payment run.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The technical stack for invoice capture and coding typically combines optical character recognition, document classification, and extraction models that run in the cloud or on premises. These components connect to enterprise resource planning systems, accounting platforms, and workflow engines through APIs, and they often rely on a queue or document store to manage volume. For legacy systems without modern interfaces, robotic process automation may be used to enter data into screens. The infrastructure must handle a mix of structured electronic invoices and unstructured scanned documents, and it must scale to peak volumes at month end.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with ingestion and preprocessing, where documents are cleaned, rotated, and split into pages, followed by optical character recognition and layout analysis to locate fields. Extraction models then pull key values and line items, and a matching step compares them to purchase orders, goods receipts, and vendor master data. Coding suggestions are generated from historical patterns, rules, or learned models, and each suggestion carries a confidence score. Low-confidence items are routed to a human reviewer, whose corrections are fed back to improve the models, while high-confidence items can post automatically.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Invoice data often contains bank account details, tax identifiers, and personal information, so access controls, encryption, and retention policies are part of the governance picture. Audit requirements demand a clear provenance trail, including the original document, the model version, the confidence score, and the identity of any human approver. Segregation of duties must be maintained so that the person who codes an invoice is not the same person who approves payment. Errors such as duplicate payments or mis-coded expenses are a persistent risk, and controls must be designed to detect and correct them. The rights to the extracted data and the models that process it are typically governed by contracts with software vendors and by internal data policies.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward fewer manual touches, with straight-through processing for clean invoices and more intelligent handling of exceptions. Electronic invoicing mandates in many jurisdictions are pushing capture closer to the point of issuance, and real-time coding is becoming more common. Large language models are being applied to unstructured invoices and to the explanation of coding decisions, though human review remains important for high-value or unusual items. Over time, capture and coding are likely to merge with payment execution and continuous audit, so that the accounts payable function operates as a single automated pipeline.
